\title{Fine-tuning the ECG-FM foundation model for Chagas screening once a recording-length shortcut is controlled: internal evidence and one hidden-cohort score}

\keywords{Chagas disease, electrocardiogram, foundation model, fine-tuning, shortcut learning, PhysioNet Challenge, generalisation}


\begin{abstract}
\textit{Objective.} Our entry to the George B. Moody PhysioNet Challenge 2025 detected Chagas disease from the 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) with the ECG-FM foundation model kept frozen. We asked whether fine-tuning the encoder would do better, and how to judge that on the public data.
\textit{Approach.} We added one change at a time to the entry: soft labels, augmentation, two-stage fine-tuning with layer-wise learning-rate decay, unpadded windows of ECG-FM's pretraining length, a hard-negative ranking loss and seed ensembling. Models were compared on a patient-grouped held-out split, within recording length, under rules written before each round.
\textit{Main results.} Unfreezing the transformer layers improved the true positive rate among the top 5\% of records (\tpr) over the frozen-encoder head it started from (\mwSseven{} vs \frozenSseven), but we could not show that it beats a frozen encoder trained to convergence; our re-created frozen entry came within noise of the fine-tuned model. Pretraining-length windows and the ranking loss together removed a length cue that is a property of the data: in CODE-15\%, the largest training source, short records are \prevRatio{} times as often positive as long ones, record length alone reaches an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of \durOnlyB, and every model we trained used it. On the organisers' hidden test cohorts, the revised entry raised our score from \extOrigMean{} to \extNewMean.
\textit{Significance.} ECG-FM gains from a short second stage of fine-tuning. On these data, none of our changes could be judged until we compared models within recording length.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Chagas disease, caused by \textit{Trypanosoma cruzi}, affects millions of people in Latin America and is often silent for decades before it produces cardiomyopathy. Serological testing is the diagnostic standard but capacity is limited, so an inexpensive test that ranks people for serology is valuable. The 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) is a natural candidate, because Chagas cardiomyopathy leaves conduction and rhythm abnormalities such as right bundle branch block and left anterior fascicular block \citep{jidling2023}.

The George B. Moody PhysioNet Challenge 2025 asked teams to rank ECGs by the probability of Chagas disease \citep{reyna2025,goldberger2000}. The score is the true positive rate among the 5\% of records with the highest predicted probability (\tpr), that is, the fraction of all positive cases found there. Training data came from three public sources with labels of very different quality: CODE-15\% with self-reported labels \citep{ribeiro2020}, SaMi-Trop with serologically confirmed positives \citep{cardoso2016}, and PTB-XL with presumed negatives \citep{wagner2020}. Models were scored on three hidden, serologically labelled Brazilian cohorts.

Several strong entries started from a pretrained ECG encoder, and they did not agree on whether to fine-tune it. The winning team found full fine-tuning of its vision-transformer foundation model better than a head on the frozen model, with a cross-validated score of 0.490 against 0.381 \citep{vansantvliet2025}. Another team, whose encoders were pretrained on CODE-15\%, found that its SEResNet18 encoder scored higher on the hidden validation cohort when frozen than when fine-tuned (0.338 against 0.231), although for its other encoder fine-tuning with feature distillation beat freezing \citep{wang2025}.
% verified 2026-11-12 against vansantvliet2025 (CV 0.490 full fine-tuning vs 0.381 frozen backbone, results section) and wang2025 (table 1).
With labels as noisy as these, fine-tuning might overwrite what pretraining taught the encoder. Or it might be the only way to reach what the disease leaves in the signal.

Our entry kept the ECG-FM encoder \citep{mckeen2025} frozen and trained a small head on its output, with age and sex concatenated to the pooled feature \citep{nguyen2025}. It scored \extOrigMean{} on the hidden test set, eighth of the ranked teams.
% verified 2026-11-12 against the official results table (rank 8, test 0.245). No denominator: the table has 39 numeric ranks (1-40 with ties), the CinC abstract says 40 and Reyna et al say 41.
Internally, unfreezing the encoder had cost us 0.08 of score, and our internal and hidden scores disagreed: a model that scored among the best on our own split, trained without CODE-15\%, scored 0.081 on the hidden validation cohort.
% verified 2026-11-12 against nguyen2025, table 3 (unfrozen/BCE 0.342 vs frozen/BCE 0.426; k-fold without CODE-15% 0.534 internal, 0.081 hidden validation, against 0.323; an SE model scored 0.540 internally and 0.079 on hidden validation).

We were not alone: across the 65 teams whose entries were scored, the median score fell from 0.279 on the hidden validation cohort to 0.236 and 0.100 on two of the test cohorts, the best test mean was 0.323 \citep{reyna2025}, and one team watched a variant gain 0.20 locally and lose 0.11 on hidden validation \citep{wang2025}.
% verified 2026-11-12 against reyna2025 (medians over the 65 scored teams: 0.279 REDS-II validation, 0.236 SaMi-Trop 3, 0.100 ELSA-Brasil; best 0.323) and wang2025 table 1 (ECGNeXt 0.827 local, 0.230 validation; frozen SEResNet18 0.627 local, 0.338 validation).
Such consistent disagreement suggests that the models learned a feature that predicts the label in the training data but is unrelated to the disease, that is, a \emph{shortcut} \citep{geirhos2020}. In medical imaging, shortcuts have been traced to the hospital and the acquisition device \citep{zech2018,degrave2021}. Here every SaMi-Trop record is positive and every PTB-XL record negative, and the winning team warned that the original sampling frequency and the mains frequency could act as cues of this kind \citep{vansantvliet2025}. A shortcut also confounds the fine-tuning comparison, because a pooled score favours the model that exploits it best.

We went back to the entry to ask how much more the pretrained encoder had to give. We fine-tuned its transformer layers in two stages, fed it windows of the length it was pretrained on, added a ranking loss and averaged seeds, one change at a time, and judged each change by a rule written down before the runs. Making those judgements meant first dealing with a property of the public data that we have not seen described: inside CODE-15\%, the length of a recording predicts its Chagas label. Section \ref{sec:data} states it, and from there on we compare models within recording length. A revised entry chosen this way was scored by the organisers on the hidden cohorts (section \ref{sec:res-ext}).

\section{Methods}
\subsection{Data and evaluation}
\label{sec:data}
We used the public Challenge training data: CODE-15\% (400 Hz; \citealp{code15data}), SaMi-Trop (400 Hz; \citealp{samitropdata}) and PTB-XL (500 Hz; \citealp{ptbxldata}), \nAll{} records after conversion to the Challenge format. CODE-15\% labels are self-reported, SaMi-Trop labels are serologically confirmed and all positive, and PTB-XL records are presumed negative because of their European origin \citep{reyna2025}. CODE-15\% contains repeated examinations of the same patient, so we grouped records by patient and held out 20\% of the groups, stratified by source and label. The held-out set has \nTest{} records and \nTestPos{} positives, at the natural prevalence of \testPrev\%; this matters because \tpr{} cannot exceed 0.05 divided by the prevalence. The other \nTrain{} records form the training split (table \ref{tab:data}). Sex and age are recorded for every record; \sexFemaleCode\% of CODE-15\%, \sexFemaleSami\% of SaMi-Trop and \sexFemalePtb\% of PTB-XL records are from women. Both were inputs to the original entry and to steps 0 to 4 of the ablation below, were removed from step 5b on, and the final model uses neither. This is a retrospective analysis of public, de-identified data collected under the approvals of the original studies, and no new ethical approval was required.

One property of these data shapes everything that follows. CODE-15\% recordings come in two lengths, and the label depends on which: \prevShort\% of the \nCodeShort{} records of 7.34 s are positive, against \prevLong\% of the \nCodeLong{} records of 10.24 s, a ratio of \prevRatio{} (figure \ref{fig:shortcut}(a)). Of the CODE-15\% positives, \shareCodePosShort\% are short records. Used alone, record length ranks the held-out CODE-15\% records with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of \durOnlyB. The hidden cohorts are all about 10 s long \citep{reyna2025}. A model cannot use what it learns from length on those cohorts.

\begin{figure}
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_shortcut}
\caption{The length shortcut. (a) Prevalence of the Chagas label in CODE-15\% by record length. (b) Mean predicted probability of held-out CODE-15\% negatives of 7.34 s (circles) and 10.24 s (squares), by model; means over seeds where there are several.}
\label{fig:shortcut}
\end{figure}

We therefore score models within recording length. \emph{S7} is the held-out CODE-15\% records shorter than 7.5 s (\nSseven{} records, \nSsevenPos{} positives); neither length nor source can help there, and it has the most positives. \emph{S10} is the CODE-15\% records of at least 9.9 s (\nSten{} records, \nStenPos{} positives), the format of the hidden cohorts. \emph{S10+} adds to the negatives of S10 every held-out positive of that length; \nStenPlusPosSami{} of its \nStenPlusPos{} positives are SaMi-Trop records, which adds power but also a source cue. View \emph{A}, all held-out records, rewards both cues and is reported for continuity. View \emph{B}, the held-out CODE-15\% records of every length, removes the source cue but keeps the length cue, and view \emph{C} is view A after perturbations of the kinds the organisers describe applying to the hidden data (supplementary note 7). Three diagnostics go with every comparison: the \emph{length-cue gap}, the mean predicted probability of short CODE-15\% negatives minus that of long ones; the mean predicted probability of PTB-XL records, all negative; and the \emph{source gap}, the mean probability of SaMi-Trop positives minus that of CODE-15\% positives.

The primary metric is \tpr; we also report the AUROC, which does not depend on prevalence. Confidence intervals are 95\% percentile intervals from 1,000 bootstrap resamples of the test records \citep{efron1993}. Two configurations are compared with a paired bootstrap that resamples the same records for both, and we report the standard error (SE) of the difference. Unless stated otherwise a configuration was trained with three seeds and we give the mean and standard deviation across them; a \emph{seed ensemble} averages the three models' probabilities.

\subsection{Model and training}
\label{sec:model}
Figure \ref{fig:pipeline} shows the model. ECG-FM is a convolutional front end followed by 12 transformer layers of width 768, pretrained on 5 s segments sampled at 500 Hz with each lead standardised \citep{mckeen2025}; as in our Challenge entry, we used the released checkpoint that its authors had further fine-tuned on labels from the machine reads of MIMIC-IV-ECG \citep{gow2023}. Leads were put in a fixed order, resampled to 500 Hz, band-pass filtered with a second-order Butterworth filter, as in \citet{hong2025}, notch-filtered at 50 and 60 Hz, and standardised over the record. The cut-offs (0.5 and 45 Hz), the zero-phase application and the two notches are ours. In the baseline the first 10 s of a record form one window, and shorter records are zero-padded at the end.

\caption{The model. Stage 1 trains the layer weights and the perceptron on the frozen encoder; stage 2 also fine-tunes the 12 transformer layers. The fixed-window variant averages the logits of $K=\lceil T/5\,\mathrm{s}\rceil$ evenly spaced 5 s windows of a record of length $T$.}
\label{fig:pipeline}
\end{figure}

The classifier wrapper released with ECG-FM detaches the encoder output from the computation graph, so we read the output of each transformer layer with a forward hook. The 12 outputs are combined with learnable softmax weights, initialised to be uniform, and averaged over time; padded positions are left out of the average and masked in the encoder's attention. (In our Challenge entry the mask was dead code, and the zero padding of a 7.34 s record was averaged in as if it were signal.) A head of dropout, a linear layer to 256 units, a rectified linear unit (ReLU), dropout and a linear layer gives one logit. The hooks, layer weights, pooling and head are our own code.

Training has two stages, with the schedule and learning rates of the winning entry \citep{vansantvliet2025}, which in its second stage unfroze all weights, front end included. Stage 1 trains only the layer weights, the demographic network where there is one and the head, for 2,000 optimiser steps at $2\times10^{-4}$ with the encoder frozen. Our stage 2 unfreezes the 12 transformer layers but not the convolutional front end, as in the encoder's own fine-tuning recipe; layer $k$ is trained at $2\times10^{-5}\cdot0.85^{12-k}$ \citep{howard2018} and the head at $10^{-4}$, with a cosine schedule and 5\% warm-up. The batch is 16, accumulated over four batches, in 16-bit mixed precision, with weight decay 0.01 and gradient clipping at 1.0. We kept the checkpoint with the best validation \tpr{} and stopped after three validations without improvement.

The loss is binary cross-entropy with a positive-class weight of 5, and positives were sampled five times as often as negatives. Targets are soft for the self-reported source: 0.8 and 0.2 for CODE-15\% positives and negatives, 1 for SaMi-Trop and 0 for PTB-XL \citep{vansantvliet2025}. For CODE-15\% patients with several examinations the target is $0.51\,y + 0.49\,n_{+}/n$, where $y$ is the record's label and $n_{+}/n$ the fraction of the patient's examinations labelled positive \citep{hong2025}. All positives were used, and negatives were subsampled so that a run saw 100,000 records in total. Baseline wander, Gaussian noise, amplitude scaling, time warping and random masking follow \citet{hong2025}; mains interference and crop-and-shift follow \citet{vansantvliet2025}; resampling to and from another rate and device-like filtering are our own. Every run went through the unmodified Challenge entry scripts, on an NVIDIA Titan RTX with memory capped at 14.5 GiB to mimic the Challenge's 16 GB card (timings in supplementary note 6).

\subsection{Experimental design}
\label{sec:design}
The work ran in three rounds, each judged by a rule fixed in writing before its runs (table \ref{tab:rules}; full texts, with dates, in supplementary note 1). Round 1 built the model up from our Challenge entry one change at a time. Step 0 re-creates the entry: frozen encoder, age and sex concatenated to the pooled feature, hard labels and class-balanced sampling. Step 1 adds pipeline corrections (the working padding mask, and a vectorised band-pass filter in place of the original signal cleaner) and early stopping; step 2 the soft labels and class weighting; step 3 augmentation. Step 4 replaces the concatenation with feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM; \citealp{perez2018}), after the FiLM-style scale and shift from a demographic encoder of \citet{vansantvliet2025}: a small network, initialised to the identity, maps age and sex to a scale and a shift of the pooled feature. Step 5 adds stage-2 fine-tuning. Step 5b removes age and sex altogether and step 5c lowers the upper band-pass frequency from 100 to 45 Hz. Steps 0 to 5c were single runs on a fixed set of 100,000 training records. B0, the end of the ladder, is step 5c with the negative cap applied inside the training script, as the organisers would train it, with three seeds. On B0 we also tried stage-2 learning rates of $5\times10^{-6}$ and $10^{-6}$, the latter the rate the authors of ECG-FM used. In rounds 1 and 2, 10\% of the training patients (CODE-15\%) or records (PTB-XL, SaMi-Trop) were held out for validation. The experiment code and analysis scripts were written with the assistance of Claude (Anthropic) under the authors' direction (see Acknowledgements) and are in the repository.

Round 2 tried to take the length cue away. \textit{Fixed 5 s windows.} ECG-FM was pretrained on 5 s segments \citep{mckeen2025}, and with 5 s windows no record of at least 5 s is padded, so the network cannot observe the record length. Training draws one random 5 s window per record per epoch; validation and testing average the logits of $K=\lceil T/5\,\mathrm{s}\rceil$ evenly spaced windows. Another Challenge team also trained on random 5 s crops and, at inference, averaged the highest quarter of the window scores \citep{dong2025}.
% verified 2026-11-12 against dong2025 (random 5-s crops in training; top-k averaging across windows, k = 25%; the paper also mentions centred windows at inference).

There is also a mechanical reason to dislike padding. In the released checkpoint's configuration (\texttt{extractor\_mode: default}), ECG-FM's front end opens with a group normalisation over time, one group per channel, computed over padded positions as well as real ones, so trailing zeros shift the features at every valid position even when attention masks them (the repository's tests show this for a 7 s record padded to 8 s and to 10 s). Pad every record to 10 s and the shift becomes a fixed function of record length that a head can read off.

\textit{Length-matched negatives.} When negatives are subsampled, they are drawn so that their distribution over three length groups (shorter than 7.5 s, 7.5 to 9.9 s, at least 9.9 s) equals that of the positives, and record length then carries no information about the label in training or validation. This is frequency matching of controls to cases on a confounder, the group-balancing remedy for spurious correlations \citep{idrissi2022,sagawa2020}; here it discards no data that training would have used, since the cap discards two thirds of the negatives anyway. \textit{Weight interpolation.} For one Challenge team a frozen SEResNet18 encoder beat its fine-tuned version on the hidden validation cohort \citep{wang2025}, and fine-tuning can degrade out-of-distribution performance \citep{kumar2022}, so we interpolated the weights of the stage-1 model ($\theta_1$, frozen encoder) and the stage-2 model ($\theta_2$) as $(1-\alpha)\theta_1+\alpha\theta_2$ \citep{wortsman2022} and scored $\alpha=0$, 0.5 and 1. \textit{Seed ensembles} average three models that differ only in the random seed \citep{lakshminarayanan2017}, as in earlier Chagas models and one Challenge entry \citep{jidling2023,nejedly2025}. Round 2 trained matched negatives (M1), fixed windows (W1) and both (MW) from B0, three seeds each.

Round 3 fixed the validation protocol. Rounds 1 and 2 had selected checkpoints on the pooled validation \tpr, which the length cue inflates, and had carved the validation set after the negative cap using the training seed, so each seed validated on different records. In round 3 the validation set is drawn before the cap, at natural prevalence, from 10\% of the training patients stratified by source, label and length group, with a fixed seed, and PTB-XL is grouped by patient when its metadata table is available. It has \rThreeValN{} records and \rThreeValPos{} positives and is the same for every run. Checkpoints are selected on the validation \tpr{} within 7.34 s CODE-15\% records, which hold \rThreeValPosSseven{} of its positives (\rThreeValPosStenPlus{} are 10 s records). The negative cap becomes a training prevalence of 6.5\%, the value the 100,000-record cap gave on our split, so that it transfers to the organisers' larger training set.

Under this protocol we re-trained the baseline and the fixed-window configuration with three seeds. Because these are new models we call them \Bp{} and \Wp. W1 was carried forward instead of MW because the two did not differ on S10+ AUROC by more than one SE in round 2 and W1 is the simpler change with the higher S7 score; length-matched sampling is therefore not part of the entry. We tested three additions to \Wp. W1R adds the hard-negative ranking loss of \citet{hong2025}: a margin-ranking loss on the logits of the top 20\% of negatives per batch by predicted probability, with weight 2.5 relative to the cross-entropy and margin 0.5 scaled by the difference of the soft targets of each pair. \Citet{hong2025} scale it by $\max(0.1, c_1-c_2)$, where $c_1$ and $c_2$ are the soft targets; we floor the difference at 0 instead. W1S drops PTB-XL, which exists only as negatives and is absent from the hidden data. The third infers over 5 s windows every 2.5 s, without retraining. Two further \Wp{} seeds tested a five-seed ensemble. The hidden cohorts are 10 s recordings, so round 3 made the S10+ AUROC its primary metric and kept the S7 \tpr{} as a guard.

\section{Results}
\subsection{The entry, re-created, and a model that reads the record length}
\label{sec:res-entry}
Step 0 of the ladder re-creates our Challenge entry in the new code (supplementary note 6 lists how it differs from the shipped model). It scored \rowZeroA{} in \tpr{} on view A and \rowZeroSseven{} within 7.34 s records (table \ref{tab:ladder}).

\begin{table}
\caption{The ablation ladder, scored on the pooled views and within record-length groups. Steps 0 to 5c are single runs; B0 and the uncapped run are means over seeds.}
\centering
\resizebox{\textwidth}{!}{\input{tables/tab_ladder}}
\label{tab:ladder}
\end{table}

All our models, step 0 included, gave short records higher probabilities regardless of label. For B0 the mean probability of held-out CODE-15\% negatives was \bzNegShort{} for short records and \bzNegLong{} for long ones, a length-cue gap of \bzGap{} (figure \ref{fig:shortcut}(b)); for step 0 the gap was \rowZeroGap. We noticed this after round 1 had chosen a model to ship: a test written when we rebuilt the pipeline had shown that the padding shift depends on record length, which varied with source, and nine days later we found it varied with the label too. Every comparison below is made within length groups.

\subsection{The ladder, within length groups}
\label{sec:res-ladder}
Within 7.34 s records the ladder is almost flat. Each step was a single run and the bootstrap SE of \tpr{} in that group is about \seSsevenTpr, so most differences between neighbouring rows are noise. The largest single step was a removal: dropping age and sex (step 5 to 5b) added \demoDropDSseven{} to the S7 \tpr, about \demoDropNse{} SE, and no step moved it by two. Ranked by pooled score, step 1 is best; ranked within 7.34 s records, the steps without age and sex are best. The two orderings differ because the pooled score rewards the length cue.

Two steps did more to the cues than to the score. Soft labels and class weighting halved the length-cue gap (\rowOneGap{} at step 1, \rowTwoGap{} at step 2), and augmentation raised the mean probability of PTB-XL records from \ptbRowTwo{} to \ptbRowThree, probably because resampling every record to and from other rates hides the 500 Hz sampling that had marked PTB-XL as a source of negatives.

The demographic input had an unintended effect. FiLM, added at step 4, raised the pooled score and pulled the mean probability of PTB-XL records down to \ptbRowFour; within 7.34 s records it moved the score by about one standard error, which at this sample size is noise. Then, once the encoder was fine-tuned with age and sex still fed in, the PTB-XL mean collapsed to \ptbRowFive. PTB-XL is an all-negative European cohort with its own age and sex distribution, and a mean of \ptbRowFive{} indicates that the model recognises the cohort rather than the disease. Removing age and sex raised the value to \ptbRowFiveB{} without lowering the score within length groups. The final model uses neither.

\subsection{Fine-tuning ECG-FM}
\label{sec:res-ft}
With the cue removed, stage 2 did earn its keep. In the round-2 configuration with both remedies the stage-1 model ($\alpha=0$, encoder frozen) scored \frozenSseven{} within 7.34 s records and the fine-tuned model ($\alpha=1$) \mwSseven, all three seeds moving the same way, and the AUROC followed: \frozenSsevenAuc{} and \mwSsevenAuc{} within 7.34 s records, \frozenStenPlusAuc{} and \mwStenPlusAuc{} on the 10 s format (table \ref{tab:alpha}). Interpolating halfway ($\alpha=0.5$) gave \halfSseven, nothing we would trade full fine-tuning for.

\begin{table}
\caption{Stage 2 against stage 1 (round 2, three seeds). ``Both remedies'' is fixed 5 s windows with length-matched negatives; $\alpha$ interpolates the weights between the stage-1 model of each run ($\alpha=0$, encoder frozen) and its fine-tuned model ($\alpha=1$). $\Delta$ is the difference from the baseline mean, with the SE of a paired bootstrap. Supplementary note 4 gives all of round 2.}
\centering
\resizebox{\textwidth}{!}{\input{tables/tab_alpha}}
\label{tab:alpha}
\end{table}

The frozen arm is the stage-1 model of the same run, a head trained for 2,000 steps, not a frozen encoder trained until it stopped improving. Step 0, a frozen encoder with a head trained for 16 epochs, is nearer the latter---it differs from B0 in other ways too---and within 7.34 s records it scored \rowZeroSseven{} against \bzSseven{} for the fine-tuned B0, a difference we cannot tell from noise. Stage 2 improves on stage 1; whether a fine-tuned ECG-FM beats a frozen one trained to convergence, our data do not show.

Stage 2 was over almost before it began. At the base rate every run peaked at the first or second epoch and then declined (supplementary note 2). Lower rates delayed the peak (epoch \bestEpLow{} at $10^{-6}$, against \bestEpHigh) but did not raise it, and test \tpr{} fell as the rate fell (\lrLowSseven{} within 7.34 s records, against \bzSseven{} at the base rate), so we kept $2\times10^{-5}$. More data did not help either. Training on every negative instead of the capped third lowered the AUROC within short records to \fullSsevenAuc{} (B0: \bzSsevenAuc), and validating every 500 steps, so as not to miss the early peak on the larger set, did not recover it; every later configuration kept the cap.

With the encoder frozen, the head weighted the middle layers most (layer \layerFrozenMaxIdx{} carried \layerFrozenRatio{} times the weight of layer 12), as \citet{nguyen2025mol} found for a different model, a one-dimensional vision transformer pretrained with masked modelling; fine-tuned, the weights stayed near uniform (supplementary note 3). We would like to read the flat profile as the fine-tuned encoder making every layer useful, but we cannot. The weights start uniform, they received a fraction of the optimiser steps step 0 gave them, and the runs that stayed longest in stage 2 drifted furthest from uniform. The flatness may be nothing more than a short stage 2.

\subsection{Removing the cue}
\label{sec:res-cue}
Both remedies narrowed the gap, matched negatives from \bzGap{} to \mOneGap{} and the two together to \mwGap. Fixed windows alone left a gap of \wOneGap. Given 5 s of unpadded signal the network cannot know the record length, yet it still scored short negatives higher, so something in the signal itself must distinguish the two formats; the recording device is a likely candidate.

Removing the cue cost us the pooled score, as it should have: \tpr{} on view A fell to \mOneA{} with matched negatives and \mwA{} with both, from \bzA{} for B0. Within 7.34 s records it bought nothing in \tpr{} (the largest change was \mwDSseven{} $\pm$ \mwDSsevenSe, with both), though fixed windows lifted the AUROC there by \wOneDSsevenAuc{} $\pm$ \wOneDSsevenAucSe. The 10 s format is where the windows paid off. Fixed windows raised the S10+ AUROC by \wOneDStenPlusAuc{} $\pm$ \wOneDStenPlusAucSe; matched negatives, which leave the input untouched, gained \mOneDStenPlusAuc{} $\pm$ \mOneDStenPlusAucSe, and the two together \mwDStenPlusAuc{} $\pm$ \mwDStenPlusAucSe. On S10 alone the AUROC was \bzStenAuc{} for B0 and \mwStenAuc{} with both remedies. By the rule we had written down beforehand, none of this was enough to adopt anything.

The fixed protocol of round 3 changed little by itself: \Bp{} scored \rThreeBzSseven{} within short records and \rThreeBzStenPlusAuc{} in S10+ AUROC, close to B0 in round 2 (table \ref{tab:round3}). \Wp{} again left S7 where it was (\rThreeWoneDSseven) and raised the S10+ AUROC by \rThreeWoneDStenPlusAuc, and this time, with the 10 s format primary, that met the rule. All three additions passed against \Bp, but none beat \Wp{} on S10+ by more than one SE. Overlapping windows changed nothing, and dropping PTB-XL did not make the positives more separable by source. On the S7 score the ranking loss gained \rThreeWoneRVsWoneDSseven{} over \Wp{} without losing on S10+, which qualified it under the second clause. By the rule as written, W1R became the entry, although its margin was only \rThreeWoneRVsWoneNse{} SE. We also took into account that the length-cue gap fell from \rThreeWoneGap{} for \Wp{} to \rThreeWoneRGap. On S10, which has no SaMi-Trop records, the AUROC rose from \rThreeBzStenAuc{} for \Bp{} to \rThreeWoneRStenAuc{} for W1R.

\subsection{Seed ensembles}
\label{sec:res-ens}
The most dependable gain in the study came from averaging three seeds. The baseline's \tpr{} within short records went from \bzSseven{} to \bzEnsSseven{} and its AUROC there from \bzSsevenAuc{} to \bzEnsSsevenAuc, about as much as the largest step of the ladder, and without resting on a single run. The ensembles also carried the fixed-window advantage on the 10 s format: \wOneEnsStenPlusAuc{} and \mwEnsStenPlusAuc{} in AUROC for fixed windows and the combined configuration, against \bzEnsStenPlusAuc{} for the baseline ensemble. The W1R ensemble reached \rThreeWoneREnsSseven{} on S7, the highest S7 score of any ensemble in rounds 1 to 3, and \rThreeWoneREnsStenPlusAuc{} in S10+ AUROC, in line with the round-2 fixed-window ensembles. Five \Wp{} seeds gained \rThreeWfiveVsWoneDEnsStenPlusAuc{} over three on S10+, which gave us no reason to train more members.

The post-Challenge entry is the three members of W1R trained inside a single call of the Challenge training script. It scored \entrySseven{} on S7 (AUROC \entrySsevenAuc) and \entryStenPlusAuc{} in AUROC on S10+, within the confidence interval of the round-3 W1R ensemble.

A score of \extNewMean{} would sit between the first and the second, but an entry submitted after the Challenge closed is not ranked, and it was built with the published methods of other teams.

\section{Discussion}
\subsection{Fine-tuning ECG-FM}
During the Challenge we interpreted our result as fine-tuning overwriting what pretraining had taught the encoder. That evidence was one pooled comparison with single-stage fine-tuning, on data where every model we have since trained reads the record length, and we did not re-run it. Measured within recording length, a short second stage helped, in the direction the winning team and the authors of ECG-FM had found \citep{vansantvliet2025,mckeen2025}, and it helped early. We also expected a lower learning rate and more negatives to help; neither did. If we were starting again on a task like this one, we would run stage 2 at a base rate near $2\times10^{-5}$, not the $10^{-6}$ its authors used, validate often enough to catch a peak inside the first two epochs, and cap the negatives. We do not understand why a third of the negatives outperforms all of them. Validating more often on the full set, which would catch an early peak, did not close the gap.

The input and the head told us less about the encoder than we had hoped. Fixed 5 s windows do three things at once: they give ECG-FM the segment length it was pretrained on, they remove the padding that the group normalisation turns into a length signature, and they hide the record length altogether. We cannot apportion the gain among the three. We do know that matched negatives, which touch none of the input, also gained on the 10 s format, so some of what the windows bought was simply the cue leaving. We did not add the ranking loss to remove the cue. We added it because it acts on the top of the ranking, which is all the Challenge score measures, and because \citet{hong2025} had used it; it turned out to finish the job the windows had started. Our guess at the mechanism is that, under the cue, the negatives scored highest in a batch are disproportionately short records, so a loss that pushes them below the positives pushes the format signal out with them---but we never tabulated the lengths of the negatives it selected. Reading all 12 layers adds only twelve scalar weights, and we would keep it, although we never tested it against the last layer alone. Age and sex we would leave out. With fine-tuning they let the model recognise PTB-XL records without finding more Chagas, and the winning team's FiLM-style scale and shift from a demographic encoder \citep{vansantvliet2025} need not contradict that: in our ladder FiLM helped the pooled score only while the encoder was frozen, and a frozen or differently trained encoder might still gain from it.

\subsection{The shortcut, and what it means for anyone using CODE-15\%}
We do not know why record length predicts the label. The two lengths probably correspond to two recording systems or software versions in the telehealth network that collected CODE-15\% \citep{ribeiro2020}, deployed in regions or periods with different prevalence of Chagas disease, which would also explain why a model that cannot see the length still partly separates the formats. The public data carry no device or site information, so we could not test this. The cue probably accounts for only a few hundredths of the gap between internal and hidden scores that almost every team saw; it raises step 0's AUROC on CODE-15\% records by about \rowZeroInflBAuc{} (supplementary note 5), and the rest belongs to cohort, label quality and device. Two of the three highest-ranked entries used augmentations that blur it. The winning team cropped records at random to between 5.65 and 10 s and zero-padded them \citep{vansantvliet2025}, and the third-placed team masked the beginning and end of records ``to simulate shorter signals'' \citep{hong2025}.
% verified 2026-11-12 against vansantvliet2025 (table 1: crop L1 in [5.65, 10] s; zero-padded to 10 s) and hong2025 (3rd of 41; "to simulate shorter signals").
Neither team described the association with the label. In our own Challenge paper we listed random padding or windowing as future work \citep{nguyen2025}.

For anyone working with CODE-15\%, the practical point is that a pooled score cannot rank models. Ours rose by \ladderGainA{} over the ladder while the score within 7.34 s records stood still, and the patient-grouped split at natural prevalence, both of which we consider necessary, did nothing to prevent it. We suggest scoring 7.34 s and 10.24 s records separately, reporting the duration-only baseline and the length-cue gap, and expecting pooled scores to fall when the cue is removed. Length-matched negatives cost nothing when negatives are plentiful. Neither they nor fixed windows guarantee the cue is gone. A pretrained encoder also deserves its pretraining format, here 5 s at 500 Hz, and a look at what its front end does with padding. Had we known about the length association at the start, we would have scored within format from the first run, and we would not have spent a round ranking changes by a pooled score that the cue was moving.

\subsection{One external score, and what it cannot show}
We have one scored entry to go on. It shows that the revised pipeline, trained by the organisers with the unmodified entry scripts, found more positives among its top 5\% than our original entry on two of the three hidden test cohorts, in the direction the within-format evidence predicted. Every hidden AUROC was below the \entryStenPlusAuc{} the entry reached on the 10 s format of our held-out set, the lowest being \extNewElsaAuc{} on ELSA-Brasil. That was to be expected: the held-out set chose the entry, and the hidden cohorts are a different population with serological labels and their own devices. An earlier network reached 0.68 and 0.59 on its own versions of REDS-II and ELSA-Brasil \citep{jidling2023}.
% verified 2026-11-12 against jidling2023 (abstract: AUROC 0.68 REDS-II, 0.59 ELSA-Brasil).

One number cannot apportion credit among the changes that separate the two entries. Between the original and the revised entry sit the pipeline corrections, soft labels, augmentation, the removal of age and sex, fine-tuning, fixed windows, the ranking loss, the validation protocol and the ensemble, and the hidden score tests the lot as a package. Whether fine-tuning alone would have moved REDS-II, or whether dropping age and sex mattered there, can only be settled by a second scored entry that differs by one change. Without confidence intervals from the organisers we cannot say how much of the difference is sampling variation either. For scale, the bootstrap SE of \tpr{} on our 7.34 s held-out records was about \seSsevenTpr.

Internally, the 10 s format of our held-out set is thin: \nStenPos{} CODE-15\% positives, and most of the positives in S10+ are SaMi-Trop records, which a model may recognise by source rather than by disease, although the round-3 gain also appeared on S10 alone. The held-out split was the selection set for every decision in three rounds, so the entry's internal scores are optimistic, and the round-3 rule, though fixed before its runs, was written after round 2 had shown the 10 s-format gain. Length-matched sampling was not re-tested under the fixed protocol. Other limitations are typical of a single study: one split, one backbone, no comparator without a foundation-model encoder, single runs on the ladder before B0, self-reported labels in the largest source, and no results stratified by sex.

\section{Conclusion}
We went back to a frozen-encoder entry to ask how much more ECG-FM had to give, and found that measuring the answer needed most of the effort. A short second stage of fine-tuning at a moderate learning rate, unpadded windows of the length the encoder was pretrained on, a ranking loss and an ensemble of three seeds made an entry that the organisers scored higher than our original one, and we cannot yet say which of them did the work. On CODE-15\% the comparison has to be made within recording length. Otherwise the length of the recording decides it.
